title: Trinity, satisfaction, conflagration, resurrection lack demonstrative light; arguments are only congruences
source_text: XXIX. Praeterea, licet quaedam, quae docet Dei verbum, sint demonstrabilia, et possint ex principiis per se notis colligi: attamen fidei multa credenda proponuntur, quae, nisi quis velit esse contentiosus, fatendum est nec esse per se nota, nec posse probari ullis argumentis necessariis et convincentibus. Sumamus, exempli gratia, praecipuum illum fidei articulum, quo docemur in una simplicissima Dei essentia tres esse distinctas personas. Quis audebit polliceri tanti mysterii demonstrationem, et serio affirmare in eo esse quandam veritatis evidentiam? cum contra ibi mens nostra nihil videat, nisi meras tenebras ad lucem illam inaccessam caligans, ut noctuarum oculi ad solem: vixque acutissimi et subtilissimi quique articulum illum possint a contradictione apparenti vindicare, nedum ut demonstrare queant. Idemque dici potest de satisfactione morte Christi praestita, de futura olim mundi universi conflagratione, et resurrectione omnium mortuorum, de quorum veritate, si quis, praeter Scripturae sacrae authoritatem, probationes quaerat, nihil admodum certi et firmi reperiet, et quod fidei nostrae fulciendae sufficiat. Non improbamus quidem pium eorum conatum qui in eo laborant, ut mysteria ista et similia undecunque quaesitis rationibus probent, et suadeant. Sed, si volumus candide agere, fatendum est argumenta illa, quaecunque tandem sint, esse tantum, ut loquuntur Scholae, congruentias quasdam, quae rem ad summum probabilem et verisimilem reddunt, non vero, quod ita sit, necessario concludunt.
pass_a_gloss: Besides, although certain things which God's Word teaches are demonstrable, and can be gathered from principles known through themselves: nevertheless many things are proposed to faith to be believed which, unless someone wants to be contentious, it must be confessed are neither known through themselves, nor able to be proved by any necessary and convincing arguments. Let us take, for example, that principal article of faith by which we are taught that in one most simple essence of God there are three distinct persons. Who will dare to promise a demonstration of so great a mystery, and seriously affirm that there is in it a certain evidence of truth? when on the contrary there our mind sees nothing except mere darkness, growing dim toward that inaccessible light, as the eyes of owls toward the sun: and scarcely can even the most acute and subtle vindicate that article from apparent contradiction, much less be able to demonstrate it. And the same can be said of the satisfaction performed by the death of Christ, of the future conflagration of the whole world someday, and of the resurrection of all the dead, concerning whose truth, if anyone seeks proofs besides the authority of sacred Scripture, he will find nothing sufficiently certain and firm, and such as suffices for the support of our faith. We do not indeed disapprove the pious attempt of those who labor in this, that they may prove and urge those mysteries and similar ones by reasons sought from every side. But if we want to act candidly, it must be confessed that those arguments, of whatever kind they finally are, are only, as the Schools speak, certain congruences, which at most render the matter probable and likely, but do not necessarily conclude that it is so.
pass_b_english: Besides: some things God's Word teaches are demonstrable, and can be gathered from principles known through themselves. Still, many things are proposed to faith to be believed which — unless someone wants to be contentious — must be confessed neither known through themselves nor able to be proved by any necessary and convincing arguments. Take that principal article of faith by which we are taught that in one most simple essence of God there are three distinct persons. Who will dare promise a demonstration of so great a mystery, and seriously affirm that there is in it a certain evidence of truth? There our mind sees nothing but mere darkness, dimming toward that inaccessible light as owls' eyes toward the sun. Even the most acute and subtle can scarcely clear that article of apparent contradiction, much less demonstrate it.

The same holds for the satisfaction performed by Christ's death, for the future conflagration of the whole world, and for the resurrection of all the dead. If anyone seeks proofs of their truth besides the authority of sacred Scripture, he will find nothing firm enough, nothing that suffices to support our faith. We do not disapprove the pious labor of those who try to prove and urge these mysteries and the like with reasons sought from every side. But if we deal candidly, we must confess that those arguments, of whatever kind, are only what the Schools call congruences: at most they make the matter probable and likely; they do not necessarily conclude that it is so.
